...Afternoon Area Forecast Discussion...

.KEY MESSAGES...
 
 - Mild and breezy conditions today with only a few sprinkles
   around this evening.

 - Isolated to widely scattered rain showers return for some on
   Sunday but most stay dry with near seasonal temperatures into
   early next week.
 
 - Increasing potential for unsettled weather mid-to-late next

&&

.SHORT TERM...
(This afternoon through Sunday)
Issued at 146 PM EDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Wedge like conditions will continue to dominate the short term 
with strong east to northeast winds at 10-15 mph with gusts as 
high as 25 mph during the afternoon. Winds will largely remain 
elevated during the overnight hours and continue to be breezy 
tomorrow. 

Relative humidity values will hover around 60% through the 
overnight hours and into tomorrow. Dry conditions that continue to
push in will limit the amount of rainfall we're expecting to less
than a quarter inch in the scattered showers that follow. The 
best chance for light rain is mostly across western Georgia, and 
some portions of eastern GA may not actually see any precip at 
all.

High temperatures today will be in the mid to upper 70s across 
the CWA with overnight lows in the 50s. Some areas of north 
Georgia will fall into the 40s across the higher elevations. Temps
will be cooler tomorrow, limited to the low to mid 60s behind the
front. Some areas in the far southern portions of the CWA will 
likely still see temps in the 70s.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Monday morning through next Friday)
Issued at 146 PM EDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Early next week will feature a brief return to dry conditions as 
the shallow 'wedge' remains in place and a ridge builds up from 
the Gulf across the Georgia. This pattern will shift quite 
dramatically by late Tuesday, as a strong trough ejects out of the
Rockies and across the Plains. Winds aloft will flip out of the 
southwest and strengthen, bringing a surge in moisture with PWAT 
values climbing from 1" to up around 1.75-2". Between the 
interaction with the wedge and the uncertainty in the timing, 
strength, and phasing of the trough as it moves into the 
Southeast, specific details of the forecast for the 
Wednesday/Thursday time period remain uncertain. At the very 
least, this pattern will support widespread rain and storms over 
our area. Any potential threat for severe weather or flash 
flooding will become clearer in the coming days. One aspect of the
forecast we do have high confidence in is that temperatures will 
remain mild (highs in the 70s, lows in the 50s or 60s) throughout 
the week. As you can imagine, model spread remains high for Friday
into next weekend, but generally has much drier and cooler air 
dropping in on the backside of the trough.

  showers and storms to most areas.

.SHORT TERM...
(Tonight through Sunday night)
Issued at 137 PM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

After a foggy start to the day, clouds will be tough to break today 
as light surface flow out of the east will likely keep clouds in 
place. Temperatures will still warm into the 70s for most with a few 
spots touching the lower 80s this afternoon with perhaps a few peaks 
of sunshine before the sun sets. It is looking like a nearly perfect 
evening to Trick or Treat with light winds, comfortable 
temperatures, and dry conditions. 

On Sunday, some patchy fog and perhaps some locally dense fog will 
be possible again, particularly over the Hill Country. Weak mid-
level shortwave ridging will arrive on Sunday, but clouds will still 
be stubborn to break. Despite the clouds, temperatures will be 
slightly warmer under mid-level ridging, climbing into the upper 70s 
to mid-80s. Mostly mid to upper level clouds will be the concern, 
but low clouds may be slow to break out west, keeping temperatures 
slightly cooler along the Rio Grande and in the Edwards Plateau.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Monday through next Saturday)
Issued at 137 PM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Monday will be yet another warmer day as clouds thin out further and 
southerly flow ramps up ahead of our next cold front scheduled to 
arrive early Tuesday morning. Ahead of this front, temperatures will 
warm into the 80s for most locations outside of the Edwards Plateau 
and western Hill Country. Instability will build ahead of the 
approaching front, but the timing of the front through the overnight 
into early morning hours Tuesday will probably limit the severe 
threat. Nevertheless, SPC has introduced a Day 3 Marginal (Level 1 
of 5) for severe storms over western portions of our area. After the 
line of rain and thunderstorms moves through, we expect cooler and 
drier weather for the remainder of the week. Cool, crip, comfortable 
mornings in the 40s and 50s along with afternoons in the 70s can be 
expected. Enjoy!

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry and cool conditions continue through the 
weekend.

Large high pressure continues to be the primary driver of the 
pleasant days and cool nights through the weekend. Expecting 
another night of radiational cooling with calming winds and 
clear skies to significantly drop temperatures tonight and again
Sunday night... overnight lows away from the coast likely drop 
into the mid 20s tonight and low to mid 30s Sunday night. 925mb 
temperatures warm significantly over the next 24 to 36 hours, up
from +3C this morning t0 +10C by Sunday evening. This will jump
start a warming trend for the week, with high temperatures 
Sunday expected to be slightly higher compared to today... in 
the upper 50s, possibly low 60s in the CT River Valley. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry, seasonably warm temperatures continue 
through much of the week. The next chance for rain likely 
doesn't arrive until late Thursday or Friday. 

Mid level ridging and high pressure dominates the pattern 
through Thursday, continuing the period of dry weather. 
Anomalously high heights and mid-level temperatures will 
accompany the pattern favoring above normal temperatures through
much of the week. 925mb temperatures ranging between +12 to 
+15C will yield high temperatures in the 60s each day. Highs 
around 70 are possible in areas with the highest probabilities 
Thursday as the mid-level thermal ridge axis shifts over. 

Ensemble guidance shows a consensus in a shift of the pattern 
late Thursday into Friday as a mid-level trough pushes into the 
region. This may be our next best shot at precipitation, 
sometime in the late Thursday-Saturday timeframe. However, there
is still a considerable amount of spread across ensemble 
solutions and deterministic guidance with respect to the track 
of this trough and its surface features. This will influence 
details such as precip probabilities, timing, and amounts. 
Ensemble guidance highlights probabilities 50-75% for 24hr 
precipitation greater than 0.01", dropping off to low 
probabilities for greater than 0.5". The ECMWF ensemble has 
leaned wetter with probabilities closer to 60-80% for 0.01" or 
greater and moderate probabilities for greater than 0.1". 
Overall, there is potential for this to be our next chance for 
rain after a prolonged dry period although confidence is lower 
in the coverage, timing, and amounts of the rain at this point.

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Chicago/Romeoville, IL
115 PM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Periods of showers and/or drizzle at times through the
  weekend. 

- Additional periods of wet weather likely next week, with
  warmer than average weather early/mid week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 115 PM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Through the rest of this afternoon and into the evening, a
diffuse zone of cyclonic shear vorticity (currently across 
central Illinois) will shift northward across the area. Some 
high-based convective cloud structures are already evident with 
this feature within zone of locally steeper mid-level lapse 
rates and resultant non-zero MUCAPE for parcels rooted above 
about 800 mb. Hard to say if forcing will be sufficient to 
result in a localized blossoming additional shower activity 
given limited hires support for this, but given the modestly 
increased instability, can't rule out some isolated brief 
downpours if sufficient forcing is realized. The lightning 
threat remains relatively low given progged ELs warmer than 
about -10 C. 

Through the rest of the evening and overnight, while general 
isentropic upglide is generally forecast to weaken, a moist
airmass with several mid-level perturbations drifting around 
upstairs will result in at least a low chance for 
sprinkles/showers persisting through the night. Through Sunday 
morning, another shortwave--this one currently pushing across 
eastern Oklahoma--will arrive in our south. This additional wave
of more coherent forcing should result in a modest expansion of
light precipitation once again, particularly for areas south of
about I-80 into the afternoon. Soundings farther to the north 
still look supportive of some very light precip, so have added a
mention of sprinkles across northern Illinois during the 
afternoon as a result. 

Much farther to the west, a long-wave trough is progged to 
eventually consolidate from several disturbances off the west
coast, including the current closed low off of the Pacific 
Northwest. Guidance is in reasonable agreement in bringing the 
long-wave trough across the Rockies Sunday night with a 
deepening surface low near 1000 mb developing across the Plains 
of KS/NE. This is expected to induce increasing, broad southerly
low-level flow across the eastern Plains and Midwest Monday. 
Best moisture return and precipitation chances look to initially
be largely along/west of the Mississippi River, though a period
of warm advection induced showers appears possible into parts 
of northern IL/WI during the day. Current NBM pops still appear 
too high across the area Monday into Monday night, although the 
areal extent has trended downwards a bit. 

Confidence then decreases moving into mid-week with the
evolution of the upper trough, and the track/trends of the 
primary surface low. Global ensembles continue to show 
significant spread in the details of the evolution of the 
primary circulation within the upper trough (the former Pacific 
NW closed low) and the degree of phasing with a northern-stream 
disturbance dropping southeast across the Canadian Prairies. 
This has significant impacts on the track, intensity, location 
and potential occlusion of the primary surface low from Monday 
night onward. At this time, it does appear that the early/mid- 
week period will be somewhat unsettled with chances of more 
widespread rain. Potentially windy and continued warmer than 
average conditions are also likely especially Monday into 
Tuesday. Of lowest confidence is perhaps how quickly the system 
departs mid-late week, and the magnitude of any intrusion of 
cooler air as it does.

Carlaw/Ratzer

.DISCUSSION /Through Saturday/...
Issued at 308 PM MDT Sat Oct 31 2026

A blanket of fog over most of the I-25 corridor and parts of the 
eastern Colorado plains made for ominous conditions to start the 
day. In fact, satellite still showed a stubborn patch of mist and 
low level clouds over Denver International Airport and its 
surroundings just under one hour ago. Despite the passage of a 
very weak shortwave over the area this afternoon, we expect mostly
sunny skies east of Continental Divide with high clouds moving in
late in the day. Southwest flow aloft will begin to transport 
Pacific moisture towards the Four Corners this afternoon, which 
will promote some isolated rain/snow showers over the high 
terrain. Areas of fog will be possible once again tonight, 
developing over the eastern plains first and slowly making its way
west to the Denver metro and I-25 corridor by dawn. However, we 
expect the bulk of the fog to remain north of I-70.

The pattern turns more active tomorrow as a closed-low off the 
Pacific Northwest coast and longwave trough extending south to Baja 
California briefly split up and then merge again as both features 
move east over the Great Basin. A subtropical jet will also slide 
north over the Four Corners with the broad wave, bringing 
precipitable water (PW) values that are 4-5 standard deviations 
above climatology for the time of year (0.60-1.00"). However, with 
such limited lift and instability, this plume of moisture may only 
amount to light rain over the plains and Denver metro, with a trace 
up to a few hundredths at most. Lee cyclogenesis east of Denver 
will bring breezy southerly winds with gusts up to 30 mph for 
portions of the east Colorado plains and Palmer Divide. Winds 
should remain light for areas west of I-76. More widespread 
stratiform rain is expected over the mountains, particularly 
Sunday evening during the peak of moisture transport. In terms of 
snow, snow levels looks to be too high for impacts during the day 
with only light accumulations possible above 11,500ft. Snow levels
will begin to lower late Sunday night as the center of the cutoff
low drifts closer to the area. 

A strong cold front will push through northern Colorado late Monday 
morning, leading to a slight drop in temperatures over the plains. 
The primary concern with this front will be the strong northerly 
winds that will develop on the backside, potentially reaching speeds 
up to 25-30 mph, and isolated gusts up to 55 mph over parts of the 
east Colorado plains. Light intermittent rain will be possible 
across the low elevations, with temperatures struggling to rise 
above the mid 50s. For the mountains, snow levels will continue to 
drop, likely reaching the 8,500-9,000ft level by late afternoon on 
Monday, and continuing to drop overnight into Tuesday. Snow 
accumulations will range between 2 and 5 inches, with the highest
amounts above 10,000ft. This will lead to periods of slick roads 
and hazardous travel conditions late Monday afternoon through 
Tuesday morning. Although snow amounts are just shy of Winter 
Weather Advisory criteria at this time, an advisory may be 
considered in the next forecast package for parts of the northern 
mountains if model guidance trends any wetter. Snow levels may 
drop as low as 6,500- 7,000ft by Tuesday morning. If enough 
moisture lingers into Tuesday morning, a few flurries to a light 
dusting of snow cannot be ruled out over the crest of the Palmer 
Divide.

Looking ahead, temperatures will remain near normal to slightly 
below normal for the rest of the work week with a period of quieter 
weather expected as an upper level ridge forms over our region.

active weather and mountain snow chances for next weekend.

Issued at 1158 AM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Southeast Texas once again finds itself in a soupy atmosphere,
with PWATs averaging ~1.70" areawide. Sfc dew points are 
primarily in the low 70s, with afternoon temperatures likely 
warming into the low 80s in most spots. It is a tropical airmass 
for your Halloween this year. Unlike yesterday, we do not have a 
robust synoptic system to provide large-scale lift. Nor do we have
any meaningful shortwaves to provide lift. However, we do have a 
weak, southward drifting boundary along with diurnal forcings that
should suffice for isolated to scattered shower activity. We used
an NBM/HRRR/Global Deterministic blend to give us our ~30-40 PoPs
(primarily along and east of I-45). PoPs are lower, but not non- 
existent, farther west, averaging 15-25% along the Brazos River. 

The water vapor rich atmosphere will only allow for minimal
cooling overnight. Sunset temperatures are expected to average in
the mid/upper 70s. By midnight, temperatures are expected to range
from the low 70s south of I-10 and w/in the urban heat island, to
upper 60s elsewhere. Not a bad temperature range for Halloween
festivities. The first two days of November (Sunday / Monday) are
looking quite warm and humid, with afternoon temperatures 
averaging in the mid 80s inland, and around 80 at the coast. 

A very active subtropical jet pattern is evident on water vapor
imagery. A deep trough extends over the Pacific well west of 
California and Mexico. A strong, moist, diffluent sub-tropical jet
ahead of the trough is pushing deep tropical moisture in the 
direction of SW CONUS. Meanwhile, a strong mid/upper low is diving
southward over the Pacific Northwest. The two features should 
phase together over western CONUS on Sunday-Monday. The 
subtropical jet will infuse the system with tropical moisture in 
the mid/upper levels, while deep LL flow from the Gulf will surge 
sfc tropical moisture northward over central CONUS. The Texas 
atmosphere should start to feel the lift from this system as it 
ejects eastward from the Rockies, with LL lee-side cyclogenesis 
expected over the plains. 

The set up described above is a heavy rain and severe thunderstorm
red flag. But if the current guidance has anything to say about
it, the overall synoptic dynamics are more likely to favor
severe thunderstorms to the north of our region. The Storm 
Prediction Center (SPC) is showing a Level 2 of 5 risk of severe 
weather over portions of Kansas, Oklahoma, and north Texas on 
Monday. But if you peer at the SPC convective outlook map, you'll 
notice that a Level 1 of 5 risk is in effect over portions of 
central and western Texas down to the Mexico border on Monday. 
This is because the convergence along the trailing cold front 
coupled with an increasingly sheared environment should suffice 
for at least some deep convection along the boundary. Thus, we'll
have to monitor this front closely as it pushes into southeast 
Texas on Tuesday We think we'll at least see a broken line of 
showers and thunderstorms push through the area on Tuesday. But we
cannot rule out a few stronger thunderstorms capable of damaging 
wind gusts. 

The air mass behind the front looks beautiful, with highs in the
70s and lows mostly in the 50s. Our northern zones and rural cold
spots are likely to dip into the 40s. Autumn should make a 
comeback in the front's wake.

Pacific Coast into the southern Great Basin. Meanwhile, to the

Nevada and northwest Arizona. With a little additional heating, 
surface based CAPE values are forecast to climb into the 250-500

expected to be as intense or widespread as observed Friday thanks 
to a sharp warming aloft and weaker wind shear, but the 
environment remains quite moist so brief but locally heavy 
downpours will remain possible.

convective to almost entirely stratiform as considerable 
subtropical moisture overspreads the region. This is in response 
to an impressive low pressure system off the SoCal coast that will
move inland through Sunday. Todays forecast guidance appears to
have converged on a common theme in terms of precipitation totals
and coverage areas - with increased confidence in locally heavy

Clark Counties. In fact, this mornings guidance suggests 24 hour

Scattered rain showers continue to spread northwards into
central Minnesota & western Wisconsin this afternoon. These
showers will begin to wane as the low level warm advection
diminishes through the day, expect rainfall amounts of 
0.1-0.25" wherever showers occur. We looks to be dry, but damp, 
for trick or treaters this evening with areas of drizzle then 
developing late tonight & through the overnight hours. Gloomy 
skies look to stick around through Sunday with little change in
the airmass expected to scatter out the clouds, however a few 
peeks of sunshine looks possible later in the afternoon. 
Temperatures will warm into the low to mid 60s despite the 
clouds, as southerly winds & warm advection strengthen through 
the day.

The main weather of note this week comes Monday into Tuesday
when a deep trough digs over the intermountain west & spins up a
surface low tracking from the central plains into the upper
midwest. Legacy physical models vary somewhat on the track of
the surface low, but the AI GFS & ECMWF solutions have remained
consistent with the low tracking directly over our area from 
eastern SD into Lake Superior. This would place the favored 
location for the heaviest rain across the eastern Dakotas into 
west-central Minnesota, a solution well-supported by the AI &
physical-based ECMWF ensembles. This will be a very wet system 
for early November with near-record precipitable, helping to 
generate a widespread soaking rain event for the region from 
Monday morning through at least Tuesday morning. Widespread 
rainfall amounts of 1-2" are expected across the entirety of 
Minnesota & western Wisconsin, with the best chances for 2-3" 
occurring across west-central Minnesota. Most of this rain will
fall within a few hours Monday morning & afternoon, but we're 
not expecting convective rainfall rates capable of any flash 
flooding. Heading into Tuesday, the system does slow down & 
linger over the Upper Midwest although models remain spread on 
how long the light rain in the wrap-around region sticks 
around. AI solutions we could have lingering showers all the way
into Thursday, although additional rainfall amounts late 
Tuesday into Thursday will only be on the order of 0.25-0.5". 
Would be a great snowstorm in another November, but we'll settle
for continuing to chip away at our precipitation deficit for 
2026.

Temperatures will remain fairly steady in the upper 50s to low
60s through the heaviest rain Monday afternoon, then we'll see
several days of classic November weather arrive as a colder
airmass settles over the region behind the system. Highs in the
mid to upper 40s will prevail into the weekend, along with
warmer lows in the upper 30s to low 40s as clouds looks to stick
around the the week. Conditions look dry well into next week once
we clear out the lingering showers Wednesday-Thursday.

.SHORT TERM...

Issued at 315 PM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Remnants of once Hurricane Vance had spread out 
and moved across the region earlier but is now starting to speed 
away to the north and east. This appears to have finally 
eroded/nudged the ridge away enough to get some rain over the CWA. 
The large area of rain to our west/southwest overnight and early 
this morning looked like it hit a brick wall as it moved into south-
central LA. Our ridge was stubborn and just wouldn't allow that rain 
to move in but it looks like it has weakened enough finally. This 
still doesn't make the forecast any easier for the remainder of the 
afternoon and tonight. 

Moisture was quickly recovering with this mornings sounding showing 
PW's already around 1.6" and GOES TPW showing anywhere from 1.7 to 
1.9 trying to push into the area. This is already around the top 10% 
so moisture is not in question. The question is forcing, lift, and 
instability. One big issue is the lack of any real focus or forcing 
mechanism in the LL. Instability may be a little higher than 
previously expected thanks to enough breaks in the clouds to allow a 
good chunk of the area to get into the lower 80s and some possibly 
in the mid 80s before we are done. A few other things that appear to 
be favorable for showers and even thunderstorms to develop later 
this afternoon and evening, one is the nose of the mid level jet 
moving into central TX right now. It should approach the western 
portions of the area around 23/00z. This doesn't look like it is 
being handled well by any of the models as they all look to be 
faster with it and farther north but tracking back for a few hours 
with GOES WV shows it is moving more easterly and not lifting as 
much and it could provide a little more lift than what models were 
thinking earlier. Second feature which has been mentioned before is 
the upper jet dropping SSE into the Gulf this afternoon and this 
evening. This is going to provide very favorable upper level 
diffluent pattern over the area between 22Z and 06Z which will 
likely lead to very efficient storms should any develop. This all 
suggests that there is still a window for more numerous showers and 
embedded thunderstorms some of which could actually develop heavy 
rain. 

That said confidence is not extremely high. Again we lack any 
significant focus or forcing feature and if that mid lvl jet does 
start to nudge more north or get blocked by weak ridging behind last 
night and this mornings disturbance then rain will struggle however, 
last few hours are starting to make me think we may have a little 
more activity than previously thought. Just mentioned the 
disturbance (partial remnants of Vance) are departing and models had 
been showing not necessarily s/w ridging but definitely some 
increase in hghts and suppression behind it but latest analysis 
shows those mid lvl hghts are not rising and and even slightly 
falling. This is likely what has finally led to some rain develop 
over the area but with that I feel a little better about that lift 
getting into the region later. With that I am anticipating a little 
more activity over the northwestern/western portions of the CWA 
especially around the BTR metro and the problem is that this could 
occur right at prime Trick-or-Treating time. Right now it looks like 
between 22z and 04z would be the time where we would see the 
greatest amount of activity. Again not expecting widespread heavy 
rain but there definitely could be pockets of some heavier rain 
possibly greater than 3" and it now looks like that could be over 
portions of SELA along and north of I-10 and into portions of swMS. 
That is in stark contrast to where the earlier thoughts of the 
heavier rain potential being across coastal MS but if we get this 
tonight over the western 2/3rds of the CWA it would likely die off 
before getting into coastal MS and then that redevelopment overnight 
we previously thought was possible would likely occur tomorrow but 
be farther east and southeast possibly completely out of the area 
and into AL and the Gulf. Still anticipate a few showers and 
thunderstorms tomorrow early but we should begin to dry out tomorrow 
afternoon with ridging quickly building in. 

Our next weather maker is already starting to slowly take shape but 
it is a complete mess right now. By Monday it should be a rather 
deep L/W trough having just crossed the Continental Divide while mid 
lvl ridging dominates the region. As we heading into Election day 
things start to pick back up but the forecast is definitely not 
clear cut and confidence honestly has taken a bit of a hit with the 
latest medium range model guidance. /CAB/

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Wednesday through Friday night)
Issued at 315 PM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Focus on the extended portion of the forecast is our system Tuesday 
and into Wednesday. Models had come into much better agreement the 
last few days well there is definitely some disagreements with 
respect o how they handle the mid lvl pattern and the multitude of 
features. This has lowered confidence quite considerably in the 
forecast for Tuesday and Tuesday night. We will still see a pretty 
decent system along with a front which will bring showers and 
thunderstorms to the area the question though is timing and 
intensity. Because of that there were NO adjustments from the latest 
NBM. 

Models are struggling with how to handle everything with respect to 
the large L/W trough off the west coast and the mid lvl jet coming 
out of the east Pac and merging into it tomorrow night over the 4 
corners region. Typically with that much wind and most of the mid 
lvl jet downstream of the trough axis it should want to pull the 
trough north/lift it out and along with that most of the dynamics. 
There are some issues though. There will still be some strong mid 
lvl winds upstream of the trough axis and then there may be another 
strong s/w diving south out of Canada Monday night and into Tuesday. 

A few different options then occur. First if that strong s/w 
develops and dives south out of Canada it would cause the L/W trough 
to rapidly close off and much farther north, over the north-central 
CONUS. This would then leave a much weaker trough axis at the base 
moving into the Lower MS Valley maybe even be held back to the 
southwest leading to a slower time frame. This also has any sfc 
reflection well north of the area and not much of a front moving 
into the region. We would still see rain and some thunderstorms but 
the risk for strong to severe storms would greatly be reduced. This 
also may keep a good chunk of Election day on the drier side thanks 
to a slower time frame. 

Another option would be if that s/w doesn't develop or is much 
weaker as it drops south. It still looks like the trough would close 
off given all of the energy that merges with it over the 4 corners 
but it would be a much broader closed low and it would close off 
farther to the southwest. This would lead to a much more defined and 
sharper trough axis and possibly even take on a negative tilt as it 
tries to move through Tuesday night. The main associated sfc low 
would still be well north but there would likely be a weak wave 
along the front farther south closer to the region. This scenario 
would continue to lead to the threat of strong to severe storms 
along with locally heavy rain. It also has more potential for 
showers and maybe some embedded thunderstorms during the day which 
would impact voting sites. 

Right now this system is still in the Pacific and with this much 
energy the models are struggling. We should hopefully begin to 
tighten things up tomorrow as it finally begins to move into the 
upper air network we start to get some better data and sampling. 
With that like was said earlier stuck with the NBM which has high 
PoPs Tuesday afternoon through Tuesday night and then tapering off 
during the day Wednesday. Rainfall amounts being advertised right 
now is not overlie impressive but those will get adjusted as well 
depending on how thins evolve. After this move through we move into 
more zonal flow and and dry out the rest of the work week. /CAB/

Scattered showers continue early this afternoon, primarily from 
central Oklahoma to the north and east (northern and east central 
Oklahoma) as a shortwave trough passes by. Rainfall amounts are 
quite light, with most locations only receiving a trace to a few 
hundredths of an inch. Even where showers aren't as persistent, 
there are areas of drizzle and mist along with abundant low 
clouds. The coverage of showers should continue to decrease from 
southwest to northeast as the wave exits to the northeast. All in 
all, its a dreary Halloween across Oklahoma and north Texas.

Fog is expected to develop tonight into Sunday morning with light
winds and a saturated boundary layer. Patchy fog is likely just 
about anywhere tonight with the most likely area for more 
widespread fog (and perhaps even locally dense) across west 
central/southwest Oklahoma into western north Texas. Temperatures 
will be relatively mild for early November (low 50s to low 60s deg
F) with some locations likely near or even exceeding their record
warm lows. 

Mahale

&&

.SHORT TERM...
(Sunday through Monday night)
Issued at 225 PM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Abundant cloud cover is expected once again tomorrow (even after 
the morning fog dissipates) with broken to overcast skies for most
locations. While temperatures will start relatively mild for 
early November, the abundant cloud cover will prevent temperatures
from rising too high, with highs generally in the 70s to near 80 
deg F. Southerly winds will increase with a strengthening surface 
pressure gradient, especially across northwest Oklahoma.

A very mild night is expected Sunday night into Monday morning 
with abundant cloud cover, breezy southerly winds, and increasing 
moisture advection. Low temperatures are expected to range from 
the low to mid-60s deg F, which is around normal high temperatures
for early November. Many locations will likely be near or exceed 
their record warm low temperatures.

Strong to severe thunderstorms are possible late Monday afternoon
through Monday night with a threat for large hail, damaging wind 
gusts, and tornadoes as an upper-level trough approaches from the 
west and intersects the dryline.

A lead wave associated with the subtropical jet stream (STJ) will
approach early during the day, followed by a stronger, primary 
wave associated with the trough in the afternoon and evening. 
There will likely be some showers and thunderstorms associated 
with the lead wave Monday morning. The coverage and duration of 
this morning activity could potentially impact the strengthen of
the dryline and the redevelopment/intensity of storms in the late
afternoon (e.g., more widespread and persistent activity early in
the day may reduce the risk of severe weather later in the day 
for parts of the area).

As synoptic-scale ascent lifts into the Plains in the afternoon, 
a surface low will deepen across Nebraska with a trailing dryline 
located across central Kansas into western Oklahoma/western Texas 
that will sharpen near or just east of the 100th meridian.

Thunderstorms are expected to develop across western Oklahoma 
into western north Texas along a dryline late afternoon into the 
early evening as the trough approaches from the west. These 
thunderstorms will be capable of being supercells with a threat 
for large hail and damaging wind gusts. In addition, with 
increasing low-level shear associated with a strengthening low- 
level jet, there will be some tornado risk with enlarged low-level
hodographs. With strong, linear forcing, these storms may

Area Forecast Discussion

144 PM MST Sat Oct 31 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- An Atmospheric River tonight through early Monday will result 
  in a prolonged, widespread rain event for portions of the 
  region, leading to gradual rises in area washes, creeks, 
  streams, and rivers at a minimum.

- Already saturated soils will result in efficient runoff and
  flooding concerns. Thus, a Flood Watch is in effect for much of
  central and eastern Arizona tonight through Sunday night.

- Isolated strong to severe thunderstorms will be possible Sunday
  afternoon and evening, mostly east of the Colorado River, with
  the main threat being damaging winds. 

- Conditions will quickly dry early this upcoming workweek, along
  with daytime temperatures slowly warming closer to, albeit 
  still below, daily normal during the middle of the week.

  
&&

.SHORT TERM /TODAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
Current objective analysis reveals broad troughing across the 
western CONUS with a strong upper-level low spinning off the coast 
of the Pacific Northwest. This deep wave will be the focal point for 
what we can expect across the Desert Southwest through the rest of 
the weekend and into the start of the next work week. Guidance shows 
the broader disturbance splitting into two separate areas of 
vigorous energy, with one area being the previously mentioned 
coastal low, with the other setting up further south over the 
sub-tropical Pacific while phasing with a strong upper-level jet.
The southern shortwave is currently helping to advect mid and 
upper-level moisture over our forecast area, which will yield 
considerable cloud cover through much of the afternoon and 
evening while also supporting a some pop-up showers, especially 
in supportive upslope areas. Current mesoanalysis indicate some 
minimal CAPE across central and eastern Arizona in association 
with peak day-time heating which could lead to some isolated 
thunderstorms as well.

These initial showers will be just the beginning of a much longer 
period of rain that could begin just prior to sunset this 
evening for parts of the region. The persistent southwesterly 
flow, which is typically synonymous with dry and tranquil 
conditions this time of year, associated with the off-shore
disturbance will help pull a significant slug of moisture toward 
Arizona and southern California. PWAT levels will approach 
1.4-1.7" which actually is not out of the ordinary as values this 
elevated are typically seen during monsoon season. However, this 
is not July or August and seeing moisture this high during the 
end of October/start of November is not normal. In fact, the 
forecasted PWATs will be around 300-350% of normal, near all-time 
records for this time of year compared to climatology. Projected 
IVT backs up the idea of how unusual the event will be as values 
will approach, and may even exceed at times, 750 kg/(ms), which 
would also be an all-time record for this time of year. It is also
not as if IVTs will peak and then quickly fall off as there could
be upwards of an 12 hour timeframe (primarily between 11 p.m.
tonight through 11 a.m. Sunday) when climatological maximum are 
seen, owing to a prolonged period of moderate rainfall across the 
region. The most robust moisture profiles will be focused 
primarily from the Colorado River Valley and eastwards, as
terrain-driven rain-shadow interference will likely result in 
some degree of drying across southeastern California, but PWAT and
IVT levels there will still likely exceed the 99th percentile, 
albeit for a shorter duration.

With that being said, expected rain totals will vary widely across 
the Desert Southwest, with an unsurprising increase in QPF from west 
to east. The greatest rainfall amounts will be focused over the 
Arizona high terrain, where persistent upslope forcing could 
potentially yield totals between 3-5", with locally higher amounts 
around the most prominent terrain features. In the lower elevations 
of Maricopa and Pinal Counties, the extended timeframe of 
anomalously high moisture levels could push totals toward 0.75" to 
around 2.5", with the higher end of that spread favoring 
locations around foothill areas where orographic enhancement of 
showers will take place. Further west toward southwest Arizona 
and southeast California, totals will generally range from around 
0.10" in the most heavily rain-shadowed areas on the lee side of
the Coastal Range to upwards of 0.75".

Even if the average forecast rainfall totals come to fruition on 
Sunday, the bulk of the rain will runoff as it will be falling on 
already saturated soils. In turn, another Flood Watch will be in 
effect for South-Central AZ starting tonight and lasting into early 
Monday morning. During this time we anticipate the potential for 
many of the washes filling or overflowing, and flooding in some of 
the larger creeks and rivers as all of the expected rain works 
through the water basins. 

Something that might get lost amongst the prolonged rainfall and 
flooding potential will be the very slight chance to see severe 
thunderstorms late Sunday morning through the evening. Once the the 
broad rain shield starts to progress further east, some minimal 
destabilization of the atmosphere may take place, which could
increase the chances for convective initiation. However, hi-res 
ensemble data shows CAPE values only reaching about 100-400 J/kg, 
which should keep deep convection fairly isolated. However, the 
environment will be very conducive for thunderstorm maintenance 
with strong mid and upper-level ascent along with 0-6 km shear 
profiles near 50-70 kt, more than enough to produce rotating 
cells. 850-700mb winds will be consistently 40-50 kt during the 
above mentioned timeframe, so strong to severe winds will likely 
be the main threat, but even winds upwards of 40 mph may get 
mixed down by what appear to be unassuming showers. Low-level 
shear will also be quite strong, with 0-1 km SRH values rising to 
150-250 m^2/s^2, levels that are rarely seen over this part of the
country. Combine that with LCL heights that will be some of the 
lowest we see in a given year, and a few tornadoes cannot be 
completely ruled out. With limited instability expected, hail will
not be as much of a concern, but if enough day-time heating can 
take place, the threat surrounding it may increase. If this
outcome is realized, the greatest threat for strong storms will be
focused from the Colorado River and eastward. Heavy rainfall
associated with this activity could also exacerbate the flood
risk. 

When showers and thunderstorms begin to clear the region will depend 
heavily on the aforementioned convective timeframe, but at the very 
least, the bulk of activity will move off to the east by late 
Sunday night. The Pacific closed low off the Washington and Oregon
coasts will serve as a quick followup behind the subtropical jet 
and initial trough axis, bringing a brief period of WAA and 
continued upslope flow for more westward-facing slopes to the east
of Phoenix through the overnight hours into Monday morning,
potentially yielding some further scattered showers. Beyond this,
rainfall will gradually trail off as even the lower level 
moisture is scoured out, and flow shifts northwesterly through 
essentially the entire column, shutting off any upslope component.

&&

.LONG TERM /MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...    
Through the middle of the upcoming work week, following the 
departure of this dynamic weekend system, we can expect dry 
conditions, and transient upper level ridging, resulting in 
temperatures slowly warming closer to seasonal levels (despite 
daytime highs likely remaining a few degrees below the daily 
normals). By late week, ensembles diverge considerably with 
respect to another upper low/positively tilted shortwave trough 
possibly impacting the region. Some solutions show quasi-zonal 
flow taking shape over the Southwest US after the transient 
ridging shifts east of the area, while others show a shortwave 
disturbance capable of diving well south of the region and 
resulting in a brief moisture return. Regardless of the outcome, 
fairly benign conditions seem to be the most likely outcome. The 
trajectory of the late week system is not favorable for rain 
chances, its residence time too short for better quality moisture 
to be pulled into the area, and if it remains an open wave, its 
positive tilt does not bode well for providing upper level support
for precipitation. NBM PoPs become introduced to the eastern AZ 
high terrain on the order of 15-25% Friday as a result, but we 
should not put too much stock in this, as the forecast remains 
highly uncertain at this time. 

&&

.AVIATION...Updated at 1750Z.

South Central Arizona including KPHX, KIWA, KSDL, and KDVT; 

No major aviation concerns are expect through late this afternoon
under SCT to at times BKN cloud decks around 5-6K ft. There could
be a few isolated showers that develop but will likely not impact
the terminals directly. Winds will favor an E-SE direction 
through this evening with speeds remaining aob 10 kts.

Considerable aviation weather impacts are expected to arrive 
starting as early as 00Z-01Z this evening and lasting through at 
least Sunday morning, with long duration SHRA and IFR-MVFR CIG & 
VIS. A few terminals may near alternate minimums and even airport 
minimums due to the low CIG & VIS by early Sunday morning. 
Confidence in sub-VFR conditions is high with cloud decks falling 
to MVFR around 03Z-06Z tonight and likely reaching IFR flight 
categories starting around 08Z-10Z with arrival of heavier bands 
of SHRA. The low flight categories may persist through Sunday 
afternoon. Winds will predominately be easterly for much of the
period, however a westerly shift will be possible closer to
sunrise as the heaviest rain bands progress through the region.

Southeast California/Southwest Arizona including KIPL and KBLH:

Aviation concerns will remain low through late this afternoon 
with light winds and gradually increasing mid-lvl clouds are 
expected at both terminals. Significant aviation weather impacts 
can be expected starting tonight into Sunday morning with a 
prolonged period of SHRA and sub-VFR CIG/VIS. VCSH/-SHRA is 
forecast to start later this evening with conditions rapidly 
degrading below VFR starting around midnight tonight. MVFR CIG/VIS
is favored, however periods of IFR may develop at times Sunday 
morning, mainly at KBLH.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER...
Spotty showers and possibly a few thunderstorms will impact 
primarily the higher terrain of the eastern districts today before
rain chances increase areawide tonight. Widespread wetting
rainfall is expected across the area tonight through Sunday night.
Minimum humidities will range between 30-70% areawide today and 
and improve further on Sunday, following excellent overnight 
recoveries. Outside of any thunderstorms, winds will remain 
generally between 10-20 mph and favor southeasterly to southerly 
directions through the weekend. Conditions will gradually dry out 
next week as the unsettled pattern departs and temperatures 
moderate closer to seasonal normals, however, humidities will 
remain above 25% areawide, and temperatures will still remain in a
slightly below normal category.

&&

.SHORT TERM...
Issued 205 PM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

This Afternoon through Sunday Night: 

Synopsis/Mesoanalysis: High pressure is centered near Lake Erie this 
afternoon, resulting in generally southeast winds across southern 
Wisconsin. A weak area of low pressure is centered over northeast 
Wyoming, with a diffuse warm front extending east-southeast from the 
low through South Dakota into southwest Wisconsin. Surface 
temperatures differences are ill-defined across the Wisconsin 
segment of the boundary, though residual warm advection and 
frontogenesis near 925 mb have provided sufficient forcing for rain 
currently extending from Platteville toward Janesville. Expect this 
activity to attempt to work northeast through the remainder of the 
afternoon and into the first half of the evening. Currently centered 
over the Kansas City vicinity, shortwave troughing will shift toward 
southern Lake Michigan tonight. Affiliated lift from the wave may 
trigger an isolated shower or sprinkle in far southeast Wisconsin, 
with other locations staying dry. Aforementioned areas of surface 
high and low pressure will linger over the same vicinities on 
Sunday, with sunnier skies allowing for warmer high temperatures in 
the presence of southeasterly surface flow. 

Rest Of This Afternoon: Anticipating that rain currently ongoing 
from Janesville to Platteville will continue to migrate northeast 
along a band of 925 mb warm advection and frontogenesis. Despite 
larger dew point depressions in the near-surface layer regionally, 
forcing within the WAA-FGEN band has provided sufficient lift to 
overcome evaporation/produce a brief period of rain. Have adjusted 
near-term precip probs to account for expectations. Accumulations 
will remain light (~0.1" or less), with an absence of instability 
pointing toward minimal thunder/lightning potential.

Quigley

&&

.LONG TERM...
Issued 205 PM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Monday through Saturday:

Synopsis: A elongated area of upper troughing will progress into 
central portions of the continent Monday through the middle of the 
week, slowly dragging an attendant surface front eastward in the 
process. The trough and surface front will pull close enough to 
influence southern Wisconsin's weather Monday afternoon into at 
least Tuesday night, when widespread rain and a few thunderstorms 
are possible. Precise pattern evolution becomes considerably more 
uncertain from mid-week onward, with a multitude of potential 
solutions regarding the progression & fate of the early week trough 
and surface front in-play. With some potential for one or both of 
the features to linger in the vicinity of southern Wisconsin, 
conditional periods of rain chances continue through the end of next 
week. Temperatures are expected to remain either at or above early 
November normals through the duration of the period.  

Monday afternoon through Tuesday: The most confident window of the 
long term forecast period opens as a coupling of low & mid-upper 
synoptic forcing arrive into the area, driving widespread rain 
potential. Expecting precip to begin Monday afternoon & evening as 
large scale warm advection increases regionally, with rain potential 
extending into Tuesday as the primary surface front & upper wave 
encroach from the west. Available medium-range forecast soundings 
hint at some weak MUCAPE through this portion of the period, so 
can't entirely rule out a few thunderstorms mixing in with the 
widespread rainfall. Tend to think that projected MUCAPE values will 
be too meager to support any stronger thunderstorms, but will be 
monitoring trends. Presence of embedded convection within an 
environment characterized by 1.3"+ precipitable water values could, 
however, lead to some brief heavy downpours in storms. Not 
anticipating a widespread flooding threat at this time given the 
isolated & brief nature of any such downpours. Initial probabilities 
from the NBM point toward 0.25-0.50" rainfall totals areawide, with 
the potential for locally higher totals to 0.75"+ where any heavier 
downpours focus.  

Wednesday-Friday: Off/on, conditional rain chances remain forecast 
with some potential for the early week surface front and/or upper 
trough to linger regionally. Whether one/both of these features 
actually do linger will depend on 1) the phasing of northern and 
southern perturbations embedded within the broader area of longwave 
troughing and 2) the subsequent impacts on the strength of the 
surface front. If upper phasing occurs, height falls will linger 
over the western Great Lakes through the end of the week, combining 
with the remains of the surface front to support continued off/on 
rain chances. If phasing doesn't occur, a tendency toward height 
rises will become favored, combining with a decaying surface front 
to support drier conditions. Neither deterministic nor ensemble-
based guidance point toward a favored solution at the moment, with 
trends being monitored for convergence over coming updates. Given 
the prevailing uncertainty, have maintained precip probabilities 
from the NBM in the afternoon update & will plan to refine as this 
portion of the period draws closer. 

Quigley

resulting in generally east to southeast winds across the open 
waters of Lake Michigan. The high will drift southeast into the 
northeastern United States through Sunday, allowing winds to trend 
southerly across the lake. Low pressure near 1000 mb will develop 
over eastern Colorado Sunday evening, progressing into the Upper 
Mississippi River Valley into early Tuesday morning. Winds will 
steadily become gusty ahead of the approaching low, approaching or

A brief period of elevated waves continues through this afternoon in

.PREV DISCUSSION...
Issued at 336 PM EDT Wed Oct 7 2026

DISCUSSION...

Pretty quiet forecast heading through the end of the work week as 
the energetic jet stream resides mostly across Canada. Stacked low 
centered over Hudson Bay today will send a trough down through the 
Great Lakes on the nose of a mid level jet streak tonight. This 
opens the door for broad troughing to encompass a portion of the 
northern Great Lakes while high pressure slides through the Midwest 
into the Ohio Valley building a stable airmass across the southern 
Great Lakes. For tonight, northwesterly cool flow over the 
relatively warm lakes will provide a boost to instability and though 
moisture is weak, PWATs roughly 0.6 inches, there could be enough 
concentrated moisture in the region of steeper low/mid level lapse 
rates to allow some scattered showers or even a thunderstorm over 
the north half of Lake Huron. Further south into the Thumb, moisture 
is even thinner and forcing weaker, but the cool airmass and low 
level jet could be enough to touch off some scattered showers over 
the Thumb this evening into tonight. Current radar over the U.P. 
does have thunderstorms present adding to the confidence of weak 
storms over northern Huron later. 

High pressure then expands back northward across the region ending 
any rain chances Thursday into Friday. Cool air within the trough 
will drop 850mb temps into the single digits above 0C leading to 
cool highs in the 60s to end the week. Clearing skies under the 
ridge with the cool airmass in place could allow some low temps to 
fall into the upper 30s Thursday night in some of the cooler spots, 
otherwise low 40s could be in store for most locations. 

Brief but strong warm up on Saturday as strong ridging over the 
Plains advances eastward over the Great Lakes. ECMWF is a touch 
warmer (~18C at 850mb) than GFS (-16C) Saturday with strong 
southwesterly flow into the region. Current forecast is for temps to 
touch 80F in the Saginaw Valley with upper 70s for most other 
locations. The warm front leading the way could touch off a few 
showers after 00Z Saturday with the bubble of stronger theta e 
lifting through the area. Though model output is not strong in 
producing rain, we've see these leading theta e gradients on 
elevated warm fronts produce narrow brief areas of showers many 
times. For now, we'll note it and see if we need to add POPs later. 

This warmup will be brief as attention the turns to TS Isaias which 
is set to make landfall over MS Friday evening then getting drawn 
northward into the Ohio Valley before getting caught in the 
westerlies and forced to the east coast. This brings the rain shield 
into Lower MI Saturday night and/or Sunday. Details will come 
together in the coming days, but for now expect a gradient of rain 
from south to north with the highest totals over southern lower MI. 
Abundant moisture with a tropical system will lead to efficient rain 
production for any areas that get clipped by the rain shield.

MARINE...

Moderate southwesterly winds gradually weaken this evening as a cold 
front extending from low pressure near James Bay crosses the central 
Great Lakes. The lighter gradient winds also veer west-northwesterly 
behind the front early tonight. However, an uptick in speeds returns 
late tonight or early Wednesday as the upper level jet deepens over 
the region. Stability trends lower with the slightly cooler airmass, 
and given the rejuvenated low-level jet winds, mixing likely 
delivers some elevated gusts. Potential exists for gusts to around 
30 knots over portions of Lake Huron Thursday afternoon, with 
marginal gusts to gales possible for northern Huron. A Small Craft 
Advisory may be needed over The Thumb should confidence rise in the 
frequency of 25+ knot gusts, but any higher end gusts further north 
should be infrequent enough to preclude a Gale Warning. Mid/Upper 
Mississippi Valley high pressure then expands into the area Thursday 
night and Friday offering weaker winds with a southerly shift.

.SHORT TERM...
(This evening through Monday night) 
Issued at 1225 PM MDT Sat Oct 31 2026

After a morning of low clouds and patchy fog, breaks of sunshine
are expanding this afternoon before a swath of subtropical
moisture feeds into NM later tonight. A few widely isolated and 
sparse showers and thunderstorms will be possible (10-20% chance)
over western, central, and south central zones through the early
evening, but instability is meager (LI's of 0 to -1 C and SBCAPE
of less than 200 J/kg) and large scale ascent will be lacking. 
These showers and storms would just produce a few hundredths of 
an inch immediately over very small footprints. Otherwise, 
temperatures are seasonable, and prevailing breezes are light to 
moderate (10-20 mph).

Into tonight, weather conditions will turn more unsettled as
upstream features come into play. A shortwave trough, currently
near 25N 130W, will be moving closer to the upper Baja peninsula
with a subtropical jet segment (45-60 kt at 300 mb) preceding it.
This will usher in subtropical moisture to southwestern states 
with PWATs soaring 4 to 6 standard deviations above normal for 
late Oct/early Nov and IVT (Integrated vapor transport) is showing
7 to 9 standard deviations above normal. Absolute PWAT values 
will reach 0.8 to 1.2 inch over many sectors of the forecast area,
not ground-breaking by late July standards, but certainly by 
early November climatology. As the shortwave approaches, the 
gradient aloft will increase with enough subtropical jet dynamics 
to instill large scale ascent over western to north central NM 
tonight through Sunday morning. This will lead to widespread light
to moderate nocturnal rain through this time with conditions 
remaining stable enough to support mostly stratiform 
characteristics. This would tend to keep rainfall rates low 
tonight through Sunday morning, but the stiffening southwesterlies
will produce orographics that would enhance amounts on the 
Chuskas, Tusas, and other southwest-facing slopes of the Jemez. 
By Sunday afternoon, the shortwave will be working into western NM
with modest destabilization occurring (LI's of 0 to -3 C and 
SBCAPE rising to 500-750 J/kg over some central areas). The 
strongest forcing through the afternoon would extend from 
southwestern NM into north central areas with convection on the 
eastern leading edge with rainfall rates intensifying as the 
upstream Pacific Northwest low moves toward NV.

The subtropical shortwave trough will slide toward eastern NM/CO
by midnight Sunday night with the next upstream trough trekking
along the UT-AZ border. This will spread strongest upward forcing
from central NM in the early evening toward the eastern border of
NM by the early morning hours Monday. While nighttime
stabilization would be occurring Sunday night, enough MUCAPE  
appears present (500-750 J/kg) as the large scale ascent arrives,
and this will lead to the development of a north-south line of 
convection that will race eastward. Plenty of bulk shear will be 
readily available, and this could lead to strong to severe cells 
embedded in this QLCS early Sunday evening (central zones) into 
late evening and early Monday morning (eastern plains). New 
batches of rain and high elevation snow would redevelop in 
northwestern NM from midnight through early Monday morning as the 
former Pacific Northwest low overtakes the Rockies. A Pacific cold
front would accompany, and temperatures aloft would drop 
significantly as the low/trough move in. This will cause snow 
levels to drop with accumulations of 1 to 4 inches forecast above 
a 9,500 to 10,500 range into Monday.

Through the afternoon Monday, the low would push into southwestern
KS with wrap-around dynamics keeping the northern zones favored
for any rain/snow, and the northwesterlies aloft would be very
brisk on the back side. This will pose wind concerns, likely
warranting Wind Advisories for central to east central and
northeastern NM, perhaps even meeting High Wind criteria (gusts of
58 mph) near Clines Corners through the day Monday. The due
northerly flow on the backside of the low would be most persistent
in northeastern NM, lasting well into Monday night while remaining
areas observe a weakening in speeds and a cessation of
precipitation.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Tuesday through Friday) 
Issued at 1225 PM MDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Much quieter weather will be on tap for Tuesday, as northwest flow
aloft relaxes and remains considerably drier and cooler. High
temperatures will remain slightly below normal on Tuesday. 

Into Wednesday, a mid latitude shortwave trough is projected to
cross northern CA and move into CO, perhaps closing into low per
the GFS. Timing differences among deterministic models are still 
posing uncertainties, but there is fair consensus that associated 
precipitation would stay favored near and north of the NM-CO 
border through Wednesday and Wednesday night. Breezes would 
increase Wednesday during the passage of the wave/low, and daytime
temperatures would remain seasonable.

Lighter west northwest flow aloft would follow on Thursday, and
then a baggy trough would potentially develop upstream of NM into
AZ on Friday. This dry and essentially barotropic upper level 
feature would slide southeastward, mostly bypassing NM into 
Saturday while a separate trough/low moves down the central 
plains. The latter feature could invoke some breezy to windy 
conditions with a cold front passage on Saturday, but otherwise 
and elsewhere temperatures look to remain within a few degrees of 
seasonal averages Thursday- Saturday along with mostly dry 
conditions.

&&

.AVIATION...
(18Z TAFS)
Issued at 1142 AM MDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Low clouds and fog that were present this morning are slowly
rising and lifting, but several locations, particularly in eastern
New Mexico, will continue to be impacted by MVFR ceilings (less
than 3,000 ft). Ceilings over a few eastern locales may not fully
lift or rise out of the MVFR category through the afternoon. A few
stray light showers and weak thunderstorms cannot be ruled out
over western and central New Mexico, but these will be very
isolated with gusty outflow winds and a few lightning strikes being
the main impacts through early this evening. A more widespread

northwestern, and portions of north central New Mexico late

Issued at 1225 PM MDT Sat Oct 31 2026

After very spotty and minimal shower and thunderstorm activity
today, more widespread rainfall will begin to overtake western to
north central NM tonight through Sunday morning, providing steady,
fuel-soaking rainfall. Most of the forecast area will also undergo
excellent humidity recovery through Sunday morning with areas of 
fog even developing. Rainfall rates will even ramp up over these 
western to north central zones Sunday afternoon as thunderstorms 
take shape. Storms will spread into more central and eastern zones
during the evening and overnight hours on a less widespread and 
more scattered basis with lower rainfall amounts. Rain will 
continue over northern zones into Monday, turning to light snow in
high elevations. Winds will turn strong on Monday, feeling much

.DISCUSSION (This evening through Saturday)...
Issued at 124 PM EDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Overview.

A quiet start to the week will gradually transition to active and 
much warmer weather by midweek before colder, drier air returns next 
weekend. A weak disturbance brings a slight chance of light rain 
tonight and Sunday, though most areas will see very little 
measurable precipitation. Cloud cover will persist into early next 
week as winds turn southerly, driving temperatures well above normal 
into the low 70s by Tuesday. A strong low pressure system and 
accompanying cold front will bring widespread rain, gusty winds, and 
thunderstorms late Tuesday night into Wednesday. High pressure 
builds in behind the front for Thursday through Saturday, bringing 
dry conditions and seasonal temperatures back to central Indiana.

Tonight Through Sunday.

A broad 500mb shortwave ridge continues to shift into the eastern 
Ohio Valley as a low-amplitude trough lifts northeast out of the 
lower Mississippi Valley. Ahead of this weak impulse, 850mb warm air 
advection and isentropic lift will continue to transport mid-level 
moisture across central Indiana.
Model soundings and the 12Z HREF mean indicate a substantial dry 
layer below 700mb, characterized by surface dewpoint depressions in 
excess of 15 degrees. HREF component members consistently 
demonstrate that initial radar echoes will struggle against this sub-
cloud dry air, resulting predominantly in virga during the evening 
hours. As top-down saturation gradually occurs overnight, dew point 
depressions will drop sufficiently to support scattered sprinkles 
and light rain showers, primarily across the southern and western 
portions of the CWA. Measurable QPF will remain minimal, with 
ensemble means generally showing less than 0.05 inches through 12Z 
Sunday.

Extensive multi-layered cloud cover and light southeasterly winds 
around 5 to 10 mph will limit diurnal cooling overnight, with low 
temperatures holding in the mid 50s. On Sunday, the weak mid-level 
vort max dampens as it traverses southern Indiana. Weak boundary-
layer convergence along an inverted surface trough will sustain 
isolated to widely scattered light rain showers through early 
afternoon, primarily east of the I-65 corridor. Weak subsidence 
aloft behind the wave should allow precipitation to diminish from 
west to east late Sunday afternoon, though abundant low-level 
moisture trapped beneath a strengthening subsidence inversion will 
keep skies mostly cloudy. Sunday high temperatures will remain muted 
by cloud cover, peaking in the mid to upper 60s.

Monday Through Saturday.

The synoptic pattern becomes amplified and highly progressive early 
in the week. A deep, positively tilted longwave trough establishes 
over the western CONUS on Monday, inducing strong downstream height 
rises across the eastern states and setting up deep southwesterly 
flow through the central CONUS. A surface warm front will lift 
northward across central Indiana on Monday, placing the forecast 
area securely in the warm sector. The pressure gradient will tighten 
in response to cyclogenesis over the central Plains, establishing a 
robust 40 kt low-level jet that advects an anomalously moist airmass 
from the Gulf. WAA will support 850mb temperatures rising to +14C to 
+16C, supporting surface highs reaching the lower 70s on Tuesday, 
roughly 10 to 15 degrees above seasonal normals.

Active and potentially severe weather remains focused during the 
Tuesday night into Wednesday timeframe as the primary synoptic 
cyclone deepens over the upper Midwest and drives a potent cold 
front eastward. Deep convective dynamics will be heavily supported 
by upper-level divergence within the right-entrance region of an 
intense 130 kt 250mb jet streak, coupled with strong differential 
PVA ahead of the trough axis. 500mb southwesterly flow is expected 
to be around 60 to 75 kt and an 850mb jet intensifying to 50 to 55 
kt with the system. This wind field generates 0-6 km bulk shear 
values of 50 to 65 kt and 0-1 km storm-relative helicity values 
between 150 and 250 m2/s2, which are more than sufficient to 
organize convection.

The primary limiting factor regarding severe convective hazards will 
be the thermodynamic profile, characterizing this setup as a classic 
cool-season HSLC regime. Deterministic GFS and ECMWF runs along with 
GEFS and EPS ensembles continue to show poor mid-level lapse rates 
around 5.5 to 6.0 C/km. Surface dewpoints in the low 60s will 
provide modest boundary-layer destabilization, but nocturnal timing 
will temper surface heating, holding MLCAPE generally within the 300 
to 750 J/kg range. Given the strong linear forcing along the 
advancing pre-frontal trough and cold front, convection will favor 
upscale growth into a linear system. The main convective hazard will 
be damaging straight-line wind gusts generated by momentum transfer 
within convective downdrafts tapping the 50 kt ambient flow at 
850mb. An isolated tornado risk cannot be ruled out within bowing 
segments or line breaks where low-level shear vectors orient 
perpendicular to line segments. Deep moisture and flow parallel to 
the frontal boundary could support localized training and minor 
hydrological issues, though rapid frontal translation should cap 
total rainfall between 1.00 and 1.75 inches.

The cold front is expected to clear eastern Indiana by midday 
Wednesday, bringing an end to precipitation and initiating strong 
cold air advection on brisk northwest winds. Broad Canadian surface 
high pressure will build southeastward into the Ohio Valley for 
Thursday through Saturday. Mid-level flow transitions to a dry, low-
amplitude northwest regime, promoting widespread subsidence and 
clear to partly cloudy skies. Temperatures will return to seasonal 
late-autumn levels, with 850mb temperatures falling below 0C. 
Daytime highs will fall back into the upper 50s to lower 60s on 
Thursday, and further into the low to mid 50s by Friday and 
Saturday. Nighttime lows will settle into the upper 30s to lower 40s 
across central Indiana through the end of the period.

.LONG TERM /SUNDAY NIGHT THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Issued at 100 PM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

Synopsis: A deep upper trough is shown by all guidance to move 
through the central CONUS on Tuesday, resulting in a high 
confidence in precip chances (90+%) moving west to east through 
the area. There still remains considerable model spread on some
details of the system, such as shortwave energy
location/strength within the larger trough and subsequent low
level pressure fields. Cluster analysis of ensembles doesn't
significantly favor one outcome over another, further reducing
confidence on outcomes such as wind gusts and precip amounts.
Mid to late week is considerably uncertain as models
significantly vary in the evolution of the pattern, with some
showing the trough or upper low stalling and lingering near the
CWA, while others have a more progressive pattern with shortwave
energy moving through. 

Winds Monday: Minimally hazardous southerly gusts up to 35 mph 
are currently expected for Monday. Given the uncertainty in the
low level pressure fields, these expectations may change with
time, but current NBM probabilities for gusts above Wind 
Advisory levels are generally < 10%. 

Severe potential late Monday into Monday night: SPC has a
marginal risk for severe weather along/West of Hwy 65 and a
slight risk over portions of our southeast Kansas counties. It
is quite likely that deep layer shear will be > 50 kts, but
instability and other near-term details remain quite uncertain.
At this time, ensemble and deterministic outputs keep MUCAPE < 
500 J/kg, with many showing < 250 J/kg. This limits confidence
in severe potential in our CWA, but many of the important 
mesoscale details are not resolvable given the uncertainty in
even synoptic level details.

Rainfall amounts late Monday and Tuesday: Overall amounts have
been trending lower, with the forecast totals now at 0.8-1.5
inches. While considerable uncertainly in these details remains,
CAM output suggests that some areas have potential to see very
little rainfall and many areas may not see meaningful drought
relief. NBM probabilities for total rainfall >= 1.0 inches
ranges from 50% over the western CWA to 70% over the east.
Probabilities for >= 2.0 inches is 10-40% (greatest SE of
Springfield). Not seeing any noteworthy flooding potential at
this time.

Mid to late week: Given uncertainty, kept the NBM blend
untouched in this time range, resulting some 15-25% chances for
rain, highs in the 60s, and lows in the 30s to 40s.

.SHORT TERM /THROUGH SUNDAY NIGHT/...
Issued at 247 PM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

A negatively tilted short wave moving though the eastern Plains and 
lower Mississippi Valley is producing clouds an occasional sprinkles 
this afternoon across our forecast area.  The wave will continue to 
move northeast through the Mississippi Valley tonight into Sunday 
morning, and is forecast to be over the Ohio Valley by Sunday 
afternoon/evening.  Low level moisture convergence along and 
ahead of the 850mb reflection of the wave will continue to produce 
intermittent light rain and sprinkles tonight into Sunday morning, 
and then short wave ridging will build across Missouri and Illinois 
late in the morning into the afternoon which will bring the rain to 
an end.  The remainder of the short-range looks dry as the short 
wave ridge drifts east through Sunday night.  Temperatures through 
the period remain mild under expansive cloud cover and light east to 
southeast flow with lows main in the mid to upper 50s tonight and 
Sunday night and highs around 65 to 70 Sunday afternoon.

&&

.LONG TERM /MONDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
Issued at 247 PM CDT Sat Oct 31 2026

The progressive, high amplitude pattern continues into next week as 
another trough moves across the Rockies Sunday night and into the 
Great Plains Monday.  Lee-side cyclogenesis forced by the trough 
produces a strong low level low over the Great Plains Monday, and 
the system moves slowly into the Midwest by Tuesday morning. 
Deterministic guidance shows some differences in the speed and 
amplitude of the trough as it drifts northeast through midweek, but 
those differences do not look to affect the sensible weather at the 
surface across Missouri and Illinois too much.  Showers and a few 
thunderstorms develop ahead of the cold front associated with this 
system on Monday over the eastern Plains and move east along with 
the cold front as it drifts through the Midwest.  Current thinking 
is that rain will hold off in our area until Monday night, and then 
will move slowly east across our area from after 06Z Tuesday through 
early Wednesday morning.  While deep-layer shear ahead of the front 
is forecast to be in the 45-60kt range, persistent clouds and 
showers will put the damper on heating and instability.  While there 
will likely be occasional rumbles of thunder Monday night through 
Tuesday night the lack of instability should minimize the severe 
threat.  Additionally, a persistent blocking surface ridge along the 
Gulf Coast will keep the richest Gulf moisture from moving up into 
the Mid Mississippi Valley ahead of the cold front.  While P-wats 
are relatively high for early November in the 1.5 to 1.8 range ahead 
of the front, the lack of instability should also reduce the threat 
for heavy rainfall as it does with severe storms.  This period of 
rainfall through Tuesday night/early Wednesday should therefore be 
beneficial with little if any threat for flooding.

The details in the model guidance diverge further after the front 
finally moves through on Wednesday, but the generally unsettled 
pattern looks to continue.  Another wave moves across the Plains and 
Midwest later in the week, though there may not be much moisture in 
the wake of Wednesday's FROPA for this next system to tap into.  The 
short wave does look like it will amplify the long wave pattern 
over the eastern 1/2 to 2/3s of the United States for Friday and 
Saturday.  This allows cooler air to filter into the CONUS east of 
the Rockies bringing highs down from the low and mid 70s during the 
first 1/2 of the week to the mid 60s for the latter half.  In fact, 
NBM max temps are likely being affected by warm bias-corrected 
guidance it incorporates, so highs later in the week may end up 
cooler than currently forecast.
